title: Who governs AI? Practical paths through a tangled global patchwork
label: 16 September 2026 · Multilateralism and AI
summary: Witnesses from Oxford and Chatham House told a Lords committee that AI brings shared global risks — safety failures, security threats, disruption to jobs and information — and that current international action is a patchwork of dialogue, regional laws and small-group initiatives. They urged using existing institutions better, strengthening technical standards and testing networks, involving companies but not letting them set the rules alone, and using UK diplomatic and technical strengths to build interoperability and capacity for poorer countries.

chapters.title: What’s the problem with AI, in plain English
chapters.takeaway: AI creates many shared risks — safety failures, misuse by bad actors, mass disruption and information harms — and these cross borders so they need international solutions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at AI in the global system. To start: what are the key governance problems multilateral forums must tackle?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Big picture: safety — how to test and agree when models are safe; security — cyberattacks, military uses and AI-aided biological risks; and regulatory interoperability — different laws in the EU, US, China need to work together.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Also cultural and language diversity so AI serves everyone; information integrity — AI can supercharge disinformation; health and science opportunities; and the environmental cost of huge data centres.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I’d group the problems three ways: shared cross-border risks (malicious use, loss of control when systems act unexpectedly, and systemic risks like job loss); lack of trusted, shared evidence about risks; and poor preparedness — we lack crisis tools to respond fast.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: All of these are linked, so governance needs to be strategic and multilateral, not just national.

chapters.title: The messy international landscape — patchwork, minilaterals and gridlock
chapters.takeaway: Lots of forums are talking, from the UN to G7 to small country groups, but different priorities, secrecy and fast-changing tech create a deadlock unless we build ‘connective tissue’ between them.

turns.speaker: Lord Ahmad of Wimbledon
turns.text: There’s a UN, G7, OECD, Council of Europe — but countries push their own models. Is there space for one global approach?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: It’s a global patchwork and frankly stuck — lots of dialogue but little binding action. The UN hosted thousands recently but produced no binding rule. We need connectors between talk and action.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: It’s fragmentary but active: UN dialogues, scientific panels, the EU’s law-based approach, Chinese regional offers, and many small-group or 'minilateral' efforts like the G7, the Bletchley follow-ups and the Global Partnership on AI.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: China pushes diffusion and localised stacks; the US focuses on frontier models. We also have export controls on chips — geopolitics matters. We need private sector involvement: many solutions depend on companies.

turns.speaker: Baroness Crawley
turns.text: Where do the hardest disagreements sit — at the user level, model level or infrastructure level?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Three cross-cutting problems: geopolitics and dual-use (civilian tools can be used militarily); company secrecy about training data and model internals; and the technology’s opacity and speed — models can surprise even their creators.

turns.speaker: Lord Lamont of Lerwick
turns.text: Will work concentrate in small groupings rather than a big UN solution?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Expect convergence in smaller coalitions on practical things, and fragmentation globally. That’s normal, but we must build interoperability so different rules don’t leave gaps.

chapters.title: How worried should we be, and what role for companies?
chapters.takeaway: Some risks are serious — misuse and loss of control are real — but alarmist 'end-of-humanity' language can be counterproductive; companies must be in the room but should not be the rule-makers.

turns.speaker: Lord Grocott
turns.text: Are we facing existential risk or something less extreme — 'killer robots' type fear?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Using apocalyptic, military or human-like language is unhelpful. It polarises debate and can push secrecy. Better to talk about specific risks and a plurality of development paths.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I’m worried — real threats include AI-enabled biological misuse and loss-of-control misalignment — but I’m also optimistic because stakeholders want to act. The Cold War analogy can mislead; this problem is spread across many countries.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie
turns.text: Companies like OpenAI or Anthropic are convening standards, but some firms won’t join. How do we get the right companies to a governance table and make action stick?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: The private sector already shapes the debate and technical practices. We need hybridity: companies in the room, but with independent accountability and state-backed rules so it’s not just voluntary goodwill.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Practical tools include third-party evaluator networks — independent experts who test models inside companies — plus clearer responsibility rules for supply chains and agents, and ways to roll back permissions if systems misbehave.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie
turns.text: But what about deployment? A firm says 'it was safe when we released it' — yet users deploy it badly.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Testing is not a silver bullet. We need ongoing monitoring, thresholds for harm, and technical interventions — like 'kill switches' that can stop or restrict models — paired with accountability for deployers.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Attribution is hard with open-source models. If a modified open model causes harm, who’s responsible — the original creator or modifier? We need legal clarity and technical tracing of agents’ actions.

chapters.title: What the UK can and should do next
chapters.takeaway: The UK has technical know-how and diplomatic reach; it should push standards and testing networks, use its G20 role and strengthen UN and standard-setting links, while building capacity for other countries.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prashar
turns.text: Can the UK influence multilateral AI rules? What are our strengths and are we using them well?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Yes. The UK has three strengths: top technical expertise (AI Security Institute), diplomatic experience (Bletchley-style convening), and strong partnerships with the US and others. But Whitehall teams must be joined up — foreign policy and tech policy must act together.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We’ve led science diplomacy before. The UK can help shape biosecurity rules, back international science co-operation, and be a bridge between the US, China and the global majority — but Government must coordinate better across departments.

turns.speaker: Lord Bruce of Bennachie
turns.text: We’ve cut aid and some diplomatic capacity. Should we redeploy diplomats to support AI partnerships overseas?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Yes — in-kind expertise matters. Work with UN agencies that help countries build AI capacity: UNDP, UNESCO, ITU, UNIDO. Offer scenario-based training to help countries prepare for AI-driven disruptions.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: The UK should also back standards development — testing, evaluation, model cards — and help countries build local models and governance so the global gap doesn’t widen.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blackstone
turns.text: Do we need a brand new international organisation to govern AI?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Not immediately. Don’t reinvent the wheel. Strengthen existing networks (AI safety institutes, standards bodies) and fund them better. A new agency with enforcement might become needed only after a major crisis.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: AI spans health, labour, security — so many UN agencies will claim parts of it. A future central agency could make sense, but it would require political trade-offs; for now, build interoperability and invest in standards and science diplomacy.

turns.speaker: Lord De Mauley
turns.text: What about China’s World AI Cooperation Organization — how is it different and what does it mean for us?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: China emphasises sovereignty, diffusion and localised stacks designed for different languages and contexts. The UK shouldn’t reflexively oppose it — we need options that appeal to developing countries, and we should seek channels to engage rather than just fence China out.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: The UK can act as a bridge, pushing interoperability at the UN and elsewhere so Chinese, Western and regional approaches don’t leave dangerous gaps.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you were advising this committee on three clear recommendations for government, what would they be?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: First, back an independent network of third-party evaluators and strengthen the UK’s AI Security Institute role. Second, use diplomacy — G20 and UN — to build minimum multilateral consensus on priority areas (biosecurity, standards, child safety, deepfakes). Third, fund capacity-building for developing countries.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I’d add: secure practical access to US frontier models for UK safety testing, pursue regulatory alignment with allies where sensible, and expand tailored UK offers for regions (Central Asia, Africa, SE Asia) so the world can both benefit from and manage AI.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both — very helpful. Any final quick point?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Be ambitious about an ideal international architecture but pragmatic: build step-by-step through standards, evaluators, and diplomatic bridges.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Act fast while attention is high. Strengthen what exists, resource it, and keep the private sector accountable — that’s our best chance to move beyond gridlock.
